title: Neuromuscular Medicine Fellowship
level: Clinical physician fellowship self-study curriculum (independent; not an institutional fellowship)-aligned independent study
prerequisites: Completed medical education and neurology, child neurology, or PM&R residency-level knowledge; this is an advanced self-study course, not entry-to-practice education.
Basic neuroanatomy, neurophysiology, clinical neurology, pharmacology, interpretation of laboratory evidence, and familiarity with uncertainty.
Clinical procedures, supervised examination and EDX interpretation are not prerequisites the course can certify; learners must not perform unsupervised procedures.
objectives: Localize pathology within motor unit and peripheral nervous system from phenotype and evidence.
Interpret the purpose and limits of NCS/EMG, RNS, SFEMG, autonomic testing, biopsy, imaging and genetic testing.
Reason across motor neuron, root, plexus, nerve, NMJ, muscle, hyperexcitability and autonomic disorders.
Use the ABPN two-dimensional blueprint to integrate disease mechanisms, diagnostics, management principles, communication and systems practice.
Critically appraise current guidelines and communicate uncertainty; distinguish education from clinical care and credentials.

units.title: Localization, phenotype and clinical reasoning
objectives: Separate central from peripheral signs; localize a motor-unit lesion to anterior horn, root, plexus, nerve, NMJ, or muscle; formulate a prioritized differential and identify urgent red flags.
topics: anatomy, motor/sensory/autonomic findings, time course, distribution, weakness pattern, sensory ataxia, bulbar/respiratory warning signs
units.casePractice: Draw a localization map and defend the top three localizations from a fictional history/examination.
units.assessment: Quiz: identify what finding would most change localization.

units.title: Electrodiagnostic reasoning: NCS/EMG and test limits
objectives: Explain what sensory and motor NCS, needle EMG, repetitive stimulation, and single-fiber EMG measure; choose a focused test to discriminate hypotheses; state timing and technical limitations.
topics: amplitude/latency/velocity, axonal vs demyelinating patterns, sampling strategy, paraspinals, temperature, technical artifacts, small-fiber limitation
units.casePractice: Interpret a fictional table of NCS/needle findings; propose one alternate explanation and one limitation.
units.assessment: Rubric: accuracy, localization, uncertainty, test selection.

units.title: Motor neuron disease, especially ALS
objectives: Apply a recognized diagnostic framework with progression, UMN/LMN evidence and exclusion of mimics; compare motor neuron phenotypes; plan communication and multidisciplinary supportive assessment.
topics: ALS spectrum, SMA, Kennedy disease, focal motor syndromes, mimics, respiratory/bulbar/function monitoring, genetics, counseling
units.casePractice: Write a structured differential for progressive asymmetric weakness without claiming a diagnosis.
units.assessment: Assessment includes red-flag investigation, diagnostic criteria, communication and uncertainty.

units.title: Roots, plexus and focal mononeuropathies
objectives: Distinguish root/plexus/mononeuropathy using sensory nerve action potentials, distribution, history and needle sampling; reason about compression, trauma, inflammatory and neoplastic causes.
topics: radiculopathy, brachial/lumbosacral plexopathy, neuralgic amyotrophy, entrapments, trauma, radiation, diabetic radiculoplexus neuropathy
units.casePractice: Map deficits across muscles sharing root vs nerve; explain what EDX can and cannot localize.
units.assessment: Case comparison: root vs plexus vs named nerve.

units.title: Peripheral neuropathy: pattern, causes and urgent syndromes
objectives: Classify neuropathy by fiber, distribution, tempo, pathology and mechanism; create rational targeted investigations; recognize acute rapidly progressive presentations that need urgent evaluation.
topics: length-dependent and non-length dependent, large/small fiber, axonal/demyelinating, hereditary, metabolic/toxic, immune, infectious, vasculitic, paraproteinemic
units.casePractice: Build a decision tree for symmetric distal sensory symptoms with motor/autonomic variations; rank tests by hypothesis.
units.assessment: Rubric rewards avoiding indiscriminate panels and acknowledging small-fiber testing.

units.title: Immune-mediated neuropathies and CIDP/GBS
objectives: Compare acute GBS variants and chronic acquired demyelinating phenotypes; interpret diagnostic criteria with clinical context; discuss evidence-supported treatment categories and safety caveats without individual prescribing.
topics: AIDP/axonal GBS, Miller Fisher, autonomic/respiratory complications, CIDP variants, mimics, CSF and EDX caveats, IVIg/plasma exchange/corticosteroid evidence distinctions
units.casePractice: Critique a fictional case against diagnostic criteria and name an urgent safety issue.
units.assessment: Rubric: discriminating criteria, alternatives, urgency, guideline date awareness.

units.title: Neuromuscular junction disorders
objectives: Distinguish postsynaptic MG, presynaptic LEMS, botulism and congenital/medication-associated transmission disorders; interpret antibody and electrodiagnostic evidence in context.
topics: fatigability, ocular/bulbar/respiratory features, RNS decrement, SFEMG, antibodies, malignancy associations, crisis, medication effects, MG consensus care principles
units.casePractice: Compare fictional MG vs LEMS vs myopathy cases, selecting next test and limitation.
units.assessment: Rubric: localization, evidence, emergency recognition, safe counseling.

units.title: Muscle disease: phenotype, enzymes, biopsy and genetics
objectives: Classify myopathy by inherited/acquired, inflammatory/toxic/metabolic/dystrophic patterns; use CK, EDX, imaging, biopsy and genetic testing as complementary evidence.
topics: proximal/distal/ocular/axial patterns, dystrophy, congenital/metabolic disease, inflammatory myopathy, IBM, necrotizing autoimmune, rhabdomyolysis, biopsy site/processing and sampling bias
units.casePractice: Choose a diagnostic sequence for fictional proximal weakness and CK elevation, naming dangerous alternatives.
units.assessment: Rubric: sequence logic, differential, selection/limitations, current evidence.

units.title: Genetics, inherited motor neuropathy, muscular dystrophy and channelopathy
objectives: Interpret inheritance patterns and test limitations; explain genetic counseling and family implications; distinguish genotype-associated syndromes without treating variants in isolation.
topics: CMT, HNPP, SMA, dystrophinopathy, myotonic dystrophy, mitochondrial disease, channelopathy, penetrance/variant classification and consent
units.casePractice: Interpret fictional pedigree and explain why a variant requires phenotype/context correlation.
units.assessment: Rubric: inheritance, limitations, consent, referral.

units.title: Autonomic, small-fiber and hyperexcitability disorders
objectives: Recognize autonomic and small-fiber manifestations and limitations of routine NCS; compare peripheral nerve hyperexcitability syndromes and relevant mimics.
topics: autonomic neuropathy, orthostatic symptoms, sudomotor tests, skin biopsy role, small fiber, stiff-person syndrome, Isaacs syndrome
units.casePractice: Explain normal routine NCS despite a plausible small-fiber phenotype; select confirmatory test categories.
units.assessment: Rubric: mechanism and limitations, no overclaim.

units.title: Therapeutics, rehabilitation, communication and systems practice
objectives: Integrate evidence, risk, shared decisions, rehabilitation, respiratory/swallowing/nutrition/cardiac/genetics referrals and longitudinal care; distinguish education from treatment authorization.
topics: current disease-modifying treatments, adverse effects/contraindications, goals, access, care coordination, palliative needs, reproductive/family counseling
units.casePractice: Write a non-prescriptive shared-decision memo for a fictional case, explicitly naming clinician verification points.
units.assessment: Rubric: evidence qualification, person-centered language, coordination, risks.

units.title: Integrated diagnostic synthesis and examination strategy
objectives: Use ABPN two-dimensional blueprint (disorder/topic × competency) to solve novel problems; synthesize mechanisms, diagnostics, management and professional practice.
topics: integrated vignettes, incidental/confounded findings, test interpretation, probabilities and uncertainty, error prevention, quality improvement, professionalism
units.casePractice: Complete capstone matrix mapping 6 fictional cases onto topic and competency axes.
units.assessment: Rubric: domain coverage, reasoning, safe uncertainty, source currency.

assignment.title: Integrated Neuromuscular Diagnostic Reasoning Portfolio
assignment.instructions: For four fictional cases spanning nerve, NMJ and muscle, submit (1) localization/phenotype map; (2) ranked differential with evidence and uncertainties; (3) focused diagnostic plan with test limitations; (4) one board-domain mapping per case; (5) a short plain-language communication and multidisciplinary safety/referral checklist. No treatment instructions for a real patient and no procedural performance. Use dated authoritative sources.

rubric.proficient: Evidence-based localization, syndrome pattern and plausible alternatives; distinguishes central/peripheral and motor/sensory/autonomic features.
Test choices match hypotheses, acknowledge sensitivity/technical/timing limitations, avoid indiscriminate testing.
Maps to published ABPN domains and cites current sources; labels uncertainty and source date.
Flags urgent respiratory/bulbar/autonomic concerns; clear, respectful, non-prescriptive communication and appropriate clinician/team escalation.
Uses only fictional or lawfully linked sources; no copying of patient images/data; no claim of clinical authority.

assignment.scoring: 80/100 is a course completion threshold only, not validated competency, board readiness, credential, or predictor of examination outcomes.

assessment.formative: 12 unit quizzes / diagnostic-reasoning exercises; 10 original practice questions above, each with rationale and linked sources. Questions are educational and not validated or official board content.
assessment.summative: Portfolio assignment rubric plus an unvalidated 50-question original cumulative quiz.
assessment.passingNotice: No cut score predicts or guarantees board examination performance; this course does not establish eligibility or competence.

topicGaps: Verified free recording ledger currently totals 7.034167 h against the 36 h video floor; residual gap is 28.965833 h. Scripted original episodes and planned clip target minutes are not counted.

Coverage is still uneven: public long-form video is concentrated in broad NMD survey, neuropathy/small-fiber, ALS trial literacy, MG therapeutics, introductory EDX and examination; these do not constitute complete subdomain courses.

Insufficient verified long-form public coverage remains for CIDP/GBS evidence appraisal, root/plexus and individual mononeuropathies, hereditary and toxic/metabolic neuropathies, muscle biopsy/pathology, dystrophies and channelopathies, autonomic/hyperexcitability disease, and current therapeutics/systems practice.

The EVMS inflammatory-myopathy recording was accessible but exact runtime was not independently visible and remains uncounted. UW archive videos are unlisted link-only streams. The named Johns Hopkins and Harvard-affiliated programmes do not disclose a complete internal lecture set or didactic-hour ledger; none is inferred.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

medical.trackType: Clinical physician fellowship self-study curriculum (independent; not an institutional fellowship)
boardNames: American Board of Psychiatry and Neurology (ABPN) Neuromuscular Medicine subspecialty certification examination
American Board of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation (ABPMR) Neuromuscular Medicine subspecialty certification (joint/cosponsored examination; ABPMR credentials eligible ABPMR diplomates)
American Board of Electrodiagnostic Medicine (ABEM) Electrodiagnostic Medicine certification (distinct examination/credential; named as eligibility by the MGH/BWH programme)
medical.boardStatus: There is a separate Neuromuscular Medicine subspecialty certification examination, jointly recognized/cosponsored by ABPN and ABPMR. ABPN develops/administers/scores/analyzes the examination; ABPMR credentials its eligible diplomates. It is voluntary and does not itself confer practice privileges. MGH/BWH states graduates may sit the distinct ABEM Electrodiagnostic Medicine Boards; ABEM is not the NMM examination. Clinical Neurophysiology certification is also distinct and is not conflated with NMM.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: ABPN pathway requires prior qualifying neurology/child neurology certification and one year of ACGME-accredited subspecialty fellowship (with specified completion timing); ABPMR has separate PM&R diplomate, unrestricted license, 12-month ACGME training and programme-director recommendation requirements. Confirm current pathways with the boards. Independent course completion does not confer eligibility, certification or privileges.

topicGaps: Verified free recording ledger currently totals 7.034167 h against the 36 h video floor; residual gap is 28.965833 h. Scripted original episodes and planned clip target minutes are not counted.

Coverage is still uneven: public long-form video is concentrated in broad NMD survey, neuropathy/small-fiber, ALS trial literacy, MG therapeutics, introductory EDX and examination; these do not constitute complete subdomain courses.

Insufficient verified long-form public coverage remains for CIDP/GBS evidence appraisal, root/plexus and individual mononeuropathies, hereditary and toxic/metabolic neuropathies, muscle biopsy/pathology, dystrophies and channelopathies, autonomic/hyperexcitability disease, and current therapeutics/systems practice.

The EVMS inflammatory-myopathy recording was accessible but exact runtime was not independently visible and remains uncounted. UW archive videos are unlisted link-only streams. The named Johns Hopkins and Harvard-affiliated programmes do not disclose a complete internal lecture set or didactic-hour ledger; none is inferred.
medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner examines a fictional adult with subacute asymmetric hand weakness and numbness. Which evidence most directly helps distinguish a root lesion from a mononeuropathy?

options.text: Distribution across muscles supplied by different peripheral nerves but a shared root, interpreted with sensory NCS and needle sampling.
Serum creatine kinase alone.
A normal routine motor NCS proves myopathy.
One isolated low amplitude proves a specific lesion.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Root-versus-nerve localization requires integrated distribution and electrodiagnostic evidence; a single measurement is not pathognomonic.

practiceQuestions.stem: Routine sensory and motor NCS are normal in a fictional patient reporting burning pain and altered temperature sensation. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.text: Peripheral neuropathy is excluded.
Small-fiber neuropathy remains possible because routine NCS primarily assess large myelinated fibers; evaluate phenotype and consider appropriate small-fiber testing.
This establishes ALS.
A muscle biopsy is always the next test.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Routine NCS may be normal in isolated small-fiber disease; test choice depends on history, examination, and differential.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which study is specifically directed at repetitive-stimulation decrement in suspected neuromuscular transmission disorder?

options.text: Routine nerve conduction alone.
Repetitive nerve stimulation.
Lumbar puncture alone.
Muscle MRI only.

practiceQuestions.rationale: RNS evaluates repetitive CMAP responses; it supports but does not independently prove a diagnosis and must be interpreted technically and clinically.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient has progressive weakness. Which general principle is essential before labeling ALS?

options.text: Sensory complaints categorically exclude all motor neuron disease.
Apply current diagnostic criteria, demonstrate appropriate progression/UMN-LMN evidence, and evaluate plausible mimics; no single sign is sufficient.
Fasciculations alone establish ALS.
One normal NCS rules out ALS.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The Gold Coast framework and board blueprint support integrated clinical assessment and evaluation for alternatives. Atypical sensory findings may call for additional explanation rather than an absolute rule.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best characterizes the ABPN Neuromuscular Medicine certification examination?

options.text: There is no separate subspecialty examination.
ABPN publishes a subspecialty exam blueprint; ABPN and ABPMR jointly recognize/cosponsor certification, with ABPN responsible for exam development/administration/scoring.
A Johns Hopkins fellowship certificate itself is board certification.
Finishing this independent course establishes eligibility.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABPN and ABPMR pages describe the joint exam arrangement and separate eligibility requirements. Training and board eligibility are not supplied by independent study.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner sees a demyelinating pattern on one nerve-conduction measurement. What is the best next reasoning step?

options.text: Diagnose CIDP immediately.
Review technical factors, distribution, clinical course and complete published criteria; assess mimics and whether findings are sufficiently distributed.
Treat based only on a borderline latency.
Ignore all clinical findings.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Peripheral electrophysiologic abnormalities require context and criteria. Current EAN/PNS criteria and clinical phenotype are used; no isolated result guarantees CIDP.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which source can be used as an open full-text starting point for MG consensus management principles?

options.text: A blog without citations.
The 2020 International Consensus Guidance update on PubMed Central, while checking for subsequent updates and individual clinician judgment.
A patient testimonial as sole evidence.
A course-generated treatment table with no references.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The cited consensus update is publicly readable on PMC; learners should verify whether recommendations have been updated.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient has proximal weakness and elevated CK. Which strategy best reflects neuromuscular diagnostic practice?

options.text: Use phenotype and timeline to form a differential, then select labs, EDX, imaging, biopsy or genetics as appropriate; acknowledge each method’s limitations.
Order a biopsy in every case before history.
Assume every CK elevation is inflammatory myopathy.
Use a genetic variant as diagnosis without phenotype review.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Myopathy classification is multimodal; biopsy and genetic findings require clinicopathologic correlation and informed decisions.

practiceQuestions.stem: What does the Johns Hopkins public fellowship page substantiate?

options.text: A 36-hour public video curriculum.
A one-year ACGME-accredited clinical physician fellowship that teaches diagnosis/treatment, biopsy and electrodiagnostic evaluation.
Guaranteed board eligibility for all online learners.
Public access to internal case records.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The institutional page states these programme details; its public page does not publish a complete lecture ledger or promise certification.

practiceQuestions.stem: A recorded University of Iowa neuromuscular lecture is named on the official public listing. Why is it excluded from counted free lecture time here?

options.text: All university lectures are copyrighted and cannot be watched.
The official access notice says viewing requires membership in a Neurology/appropriate hospital group or alumni; it is therefore not verified public free access for this curriculum.
Its duration is necessarily zero.
It is a research-only specialty.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The public access notice establishes the restriction; this project neither sought login nor bypassed it.

assignment.title: Structured neuropathology consultation and evidence map
assignment.instructions: Select one case linked from Pittsburgh CPC materials only if the specific presentation is demonstrably de-identified and its use conditions permit viewing; otherwise create a fictional vignette and do not use patient images. Submit specimen/context summary, low-to-high power morphology, ranked differential, selected ancillary tests with purpose/limits, integrated or provisional report, one uncertainty statement and five linked evidence sources. Do not copy/rehost case slides or reproduce protected patient information.

assessment.rubric: Credit reasoning, source citation, uncertainty and safe limits over unsupported entity naming. These original questions are educational, not official ABPath items or a validated readiness/passing predictor. No score implies competence or eligibility.

studyHours.basis: Transparent learner plan, not an observed runtime: 13.85 h assigned public videos (10.34 specialty + 0.90 general foundation + 2.61 supplemental), approximately 24 h open reading, 36 h case/slide study, 27 h quizzes and assignments, 19 h revision. It does not fill the 36-hour specialty-video minimum; planned clips do not count.

mapping.institution: Johns Hopkins School of Medicine / Johns Hopkins Hospital
mapping.name: Neuropathology Fellowship (diagnostic clinical training pathway; institution describes a two-year fellowship linked from its curriculum; separate JH Medicine directory entry says 2 years and ACGME Accredited)
mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: The separate official Pathology curriculum says residents completing AP, AP/CP, or neuro-related clinical training (including one year of AP) apply directly to a two-year fellowship and describes core NP rotations (autopsy, surgical NP, muscle/nerve, ophthalmic, pediatric elective) and weekly conferences. The linked Hopkins Pathology “Neuropathology Fellowship” page at /education/fellowships/neuropathology instead foregrounds an experimental/research fellowship for physician and PhD investigators. Preserve this institutional page-level discrepancy; do not conflate research fellowship with diagnostic training.

mapping.institution: Johns Hopkins School of Medicine / Johns Hopkins Hospital

Count as research-track institutional offering, not the clinical curriculum itself.

medical.trackType: Clinical physician fellowship curriculum (with separate integrated AP/NP and research-track institutional variants documented)
boardNames: American Board of Pathology (ABPath) Neuropathology subspecialty certification
ABPath combined Anatomic Pathology/Neuropathology (AP/NP) pathway/certificate (institutional residency variant; individual eligibility must be confirmed)
medical.boardStatus: A distinct ABPath Neuropathology subspecialty examination exists (168 written/practical questions plus 62 virtual microscopy questions; 6 h 12 min). Hopkins also describes AP/NP primary board eligibility for its integrated residency pathway. Board eligibility is individual and is not conferred by this independent course.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: ABPath rules require qualifying medical education, unrestricted licensure, primary/other ABMS certification for subspecialty examination eligibility and qualifying training/autopsy requirements as applicable. ACGME program-entry exceptions do not guarantee certification eligibility. Verify current individual eligibility directly with ABPath. This course grants no eligibility.

officialProgrammes.institution: Johns Hopkins School of Medicine / Johns Hopkins Hospital
officialProgrammes.name: Neuropathology Fellowship (diagnostic clinical training pathway; institution describes a two-year fellowship linked from its curriculum; separate JH Medicine directory entry says 2 years and ACGME Accredited)
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: The separate official Pathology curriculum says residents completing AP, AP/CP, or neuro-related clinical training (including one year of AP) apply directly to a two-year fellowship and describes core NP rotations (autopsy, surgical NP, muscle/nerve, ophthalmic, pediatric elective) and weekly conferences. The linked Hopkins Pathology “Neuropathology Fellowship” page at /education/fellowships/neuropathology instead foregrounds an experimental/research fellowship for physician and PhD investigators. Preserve this institutional page-level discrepancy; do not conflate research fellowship with diagnostic training.

officialProgrammes.institution: Johns Hopkins School of Medicine / Johns Hopkins Hospital
officialProgrammes.name: Integrated AP/NP residency pathway (associated physician-training variant; not a separate fellowship)
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official curriculum lists four-year integrated AP/NP training; two initial AP years followed by two NP fellowship years, with up to 21 months NP rotations and a final-year elective/research period. It states AP/NP Board eligibility; this is an institutional pathway, not a substitute for individual ABPath eligibility determination.

officialProgrammes.name: Experimental Neuropathology Fellowship (research track; distinct from diagnostic clinical track)
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official page explicitly calls this experimental, describes basic-science research for MD/MD-PhD/PhD investigators, and says separate residency training leading to neuropathology board eligibility is available. Count as research-track institutional offering, not the clinical curriculum itself.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Johns Hopkins-affiliated institutional pages only; exact distinctions preserved between diagnostic clinical fellowship, integrated AP/NP residency pathway, and experimental research fellowship. Johns Hopkins Medicine directory entry labels a two-year ACGME-accredited fellowship, while the linked main Pathology fellowship page primarily describes an experimental fellowship; its residency curriculum explicitly points to a separate two-year clinical training pathway. Do not equate the research category with diagnostic board-training.
sourceCaveats: Johns Hopkins pages disagree in emphasis and naming: the directory calls the 2-year program ACGME-accredited; the official fellowship page describes an experimental/research track; the official residency curriculum separately documents a diagnostic clinical fellowship and AP/NP residency route. We preserve all three and do not invent a consolidated syllabus.

The 2024 ABPath neuropathology content specifications are labeled a draft general guide for 2025 exams; the board page links a 2026 exam blueprint that was not fully extractable during this research. Re-check current board documents before study or practice.
ACGME program entry, clinical training, and ABPath examination eligibility are distinct; program completion alone does not guarantee board eligibility.

No human clinical review performed. Course is independent and unaffiliated; no accredited training, licensure, board eligibility, professional certification, procedure competence or guaranteed passing is provided.
No protected exam items, patient records or images were copied. Public resources are links only; case-level de-identification/reuse rights may be unverified.

practiceQuestions.stem: A cerebral hemispheric diffuse glioma in an adult has infiltrating astrocytic morphology. Testing shows an IDH mutation and whole-arm 1p/19q codeletion. Under WHO CNS5, which integrated type best fits?

options.text: Astrocytoma, IDH-mutant
Oligodendroglioma, IDH-mutant, and 1p/19q-codeleted
Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype
Diffuse midline glioma, H3 K27-altered

practiceQuestions.rationale: WHO CNS5 defines oligodendroglioma by IDH mutation plus whole-arm 1p/19q codeletion; integrated diagnosis uses morphology and molecular features, not morphology alone.

practiceQuestions.stem: In a fictional teaching specimen, a high-grade adult diffuse glioma is IDH-wildtype and has necrosis and microvascular proliferation. Which WHO CNS5 entity is most consistent, assuming the full diagnostic context supports it?

options.text: Astrocytoma, IDH-mutant, grade 4
Oligodendroglioma, IDH-mutant, and 1p/19q-codeleted
Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype
Pilocytic astrocytoma

practiceQuestions.rationale: The described high-grade morphology in an IDH-wildtype adult diffuse glioma is consistent with glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype; real integrated sign-out must consider defining molecular criteria and the complete context.

practiceQuestions.stem: A pediatric diffuse midline tumor has H3 K27 alteration. Which general classification principle should be applied?

options.text: Use the integrated entity name and include the relevant molecular context
Classify as adult-type glioblastoma solely by grade
Ignore the anatomic site
Diagnose solely by radiology

practiceQuestions.rationale: WHO CNS5 recognizes diffuse midline glioma, H3 K27-altered; site and molecular context are integral to classification.

practiceQuestions.stem: A cortical specimen from a patient with drug-resistant focal seizures shows a circumscribed dysplastic neuronal-glial lesion. What is the safest next reasoning step?

options.text: Assign a unique tumor without clinical or molecular correlation
Integrate age, seizure history, site, morphology and any indicated ancillary tests
Assume every seizure-associated lesion is ganglioglioma
Use radiology as the tissue diagnosis

practiceQuestions.rationale: Epilepsy-associated lesions require clinicopathologic integration; the vignette is intentionally under-specified for a single entity.

practiceQuestions.stem: A white-matter lesion shows loss of myelin with relative preservation of axons in the sampled active area. Which broad process does this pattern favor?

options.text: Primary demyelination
Pure axonal transection
Meningioma
Prion spongiform change

practiceQuestions.rationale: Relative axonal preservation with myelin loss supports demyelination, but clinical, distributional and ancillary evidence is needed for specific etiology.

practiceQuestions.stem: What is the most defensible response to a small biopsy with crush artifact and scant viable tissue?

options.text: Issue a definitive integrated classification based on one nonspecific stain
Describe limitations, triage remaining tissue, and recommend clinically appropriate correlation/testing
Infer tumor grade from specimen size
State that molecular testing is always unnecessary

practiceQuestions.rationale: Specimen adequacy, artifact and tissue stewardship affect interpretation; transparent limitations are a core consult skill.

practiceQuestions.stem: A teaching autopsy brain shows neuronal loss, reactive gliosis and spongiform vacuolation in gray matter. Which disease family is a key differential that warrants appropriate prion-protein evaluation?

options.text: Prion disease
Oligodendroglioma
Meningioma
Peripheral neuropathy

practiceQuestions.rationale: Spongiform change with neuronal loss and gliosis is a classic neuropathologic pattern of prion disease; this pattern is not by itself a final etiologic diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.stem: A case has a distinctive morphology but discordant molecular data. Under the WHO CNS5 integrated-diagnosis framework, what is the best approach?

options.text: Report the morphology-only entity as final regardless of molecular conflict
Reconcile quality, method and differential; report uncertainty or ancillary-test limitations rather than force an integrated label
Ignore all molecular results
Use a research classifier as a substitute for expert interpretation

practiceQuestions.rationale: WHO CNS5 emphasizes integrated, layered classification using established methods; discordance requires review and calibrated uncertainty.

practiceQuestions.stem: For an educational digital pathology classifier, which validation concern is most important before using its output?

options.text: Whether training/test data are independent and representative, and whether performance is validated for intended use
The slide viewer color theme only
Whether it produces a fluent explanation
Whether it replaces pathologist review

practiceQuestions.rationale: Model performance depends on dataset independence, representativeness, workflow and external validation; AI output is decision support, not autonomous diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fellow accepted under an ACGME program eligibility exception completes training. What can be inferred about ABPath certification eligibility?

options.text: Eligibility is automatic after any ACGME fellowship
The candidate should verify individual requirements directly with ABPath; ACGME entry exceptions do not guarantee board eligibility
The program director can waive board rules
A research fellowship is equivalent to a board certificate

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACGME FAQ explicitly states acceptance under the fellow eligibility exception does not guarantee ABPath certification eligibility.

officialProgrammes.name: Neuroplastic and Reconstructive Surgery Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Current official page describes a one-year fellowship, one position/year, for physicians who have completed an ACGME-approved plastic-surgery residency; clinical focus is adult craniomaxillofacial and neurocranial reconstruction. Partnership is between Johns Hopkins Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery and Neurosurgery; successful completion yields a graduation certificate signed by both departments. Named collaborating disciplines and translational research are described, but a rotation schedule, case volume, assessment blueprint, and complete didactic lecture curriculum are not published. The original packet URL is preserved as sourceListedUrl; the current official canonical page is used here.

institutionVariants: Johns Hopkins School of Medicine — Neuroplastic and Reconstructive Surgery Fellowship (the single offering in the packet). No additional Harvard-affiliated or Johns Hopkins variant identified for this exact programme name.
programmeSourceScope.classification: Actual physician clinical fellowship: Hopkins describes clinical treatment of adult injury, deformity, tumor, or trauma affecting face/skull. It is a one-year, post-residency fellowship, not a residency or combined residency. It partners across two departments; not a combined board programme. Translational research is one component, not a research-only postdoc. The broader Hopkins Neuroplastic Approach page mentions both adult and pediatric service populations, while the fellowship page specifies adult focus; those scopes are not conflated.
programmeSourceScope.accreditation: The fellowship page establishes an ACGME-approved plastic surgery residency prerequisite, not that this fellowship is itself ACGME-accredited. The 2026 ACGME plastic-surgery requirements page lists plastic surgery, craniofacial plastic surgery, and hand surgery requirements; no Neuroplastic and Reconstructive Surgery fellowship requirement was found there. The generic directory label “ACGME Accredited or Equivalent” is not treated as per-program accreditation evidence. A live ADS program-status determination was not obtained.
programmeSourceScope.boards: ABMS recognizes ABPS for Plastic Surgery and a Plastic Surgery Within the Head and Neck subspecialty. No independent neuroplastic board/exam was identified. Fellowship graduation certificate is separate from board certification.
programmeSourceScope.publicTrainingDetails: Official page lists one available position/year, multidisciplinary work alongside neurosurgery, plastic surgery, hematology, infectious disease, medical and radiation neuro-oncology, PM&R, and head-and-neck surgery. Translational collaboration with JHU Applied Physics Laboratory and Walter Reed is described. Public page does not enumerate formal rotations, cases, exact training hours, outcomes, or procedures.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement is best supported by the current Johns Hopkins fellowship page?

options.text: A two-year ACGME-accredited combined residency in plastic surgery and neurosurgery.
A one-year physician fellowship focused on adult craniomaxillofacial and neurocranial reconstruction, in partnership between two departments.
A research-only postdoctoral job without clinical work.
A pediatric craniofacial fellowship offered at all Harvard-affiliated hospitals.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The official page describes a one-year fellowship, the adult clinical focus, and the Department of Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery/Department of Neurosurgery partnership. It does not call it a combined residency or research-only role.

practiceQuestions.stem: What does the official fellowship page state is the entry prerequisite?

options.text: Completion of an ACGME-approved plastic surgery residency.
An ABMS certificate in neuroplastic surgery.
A prior craniofacial fellowship and a public board examination.
A minimum published number of cranial implant cases.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Hopkins says applicants have completed a plastic surgery residency approved by ACGME. No neuroplastic-specific board exam or case-volume eligibility threshold is stated on the page.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which is the most accurate board statement?

options.text: Completing the Hopkins fellowship automatically awards ABPS certification.
Neuroplastic and Reconstructive Surgery has a separate ABMS member board and exam.
ABPS is the relevant plastic-surgery board context; no separate neuroplastic fellowship exam was identified, and a Hopkins completion certificate is not board certification.
The fellowship awards certification in neurosurgery.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABMS lists ABPS and a head-and-neck plastic surgery subspecialty; Hopkins describes a two-department graduation certificate. No evidence indicates a distinct neuroplastic board or automatic ABPS certification.

practiceQuestions.stem: The 2022 review of alloplastic cranioplasty materials supports which conclusion?

options.text: One implant material is best for all adults.
Material selection should be individualized; the review describes patient/defect trade-offs and is nonsystematic.
All autologous bone should be rejected.
Cost is the only relevant material consideration.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The review explicitly notes material choice depends on defect and patient factors, and describes itself as a nonsystematic literature review. No universally preferred material is established.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which goal is included among potential aims of cranioplasty in the open review?

options.text: Cosmetic appearance only; intracranial protection is unrelated.
Protection of intracranial structures and improved cosmesis, with neurologic or rehabilitative benefits considered cautiously.
Guaranteed reversal of all deficits after craniectomy.
Prevention of every later seizure.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The review describes intracranial protection and cosmesis; potential neurocognitive/rehabilitation effects should not be promised because outcomes and evidence vary.

practiceQuestions.stem: Fictional adult patient A has an acquired cranial defect after decompressive surgery, a wound complication under assessment, and a CSF device. What is the best educational response?

options.text: Apply a fixed interval from craniectomy that is correct for every patient.
Use the same material used in the largest retrospective series.
Structure multidisciplinary assessment of wound/device status, defect/soft tissues, goals, and evidence limits; do not prescribe a universal timing rule.
Declare a syndrome of trephined before reconstruction from the defect alone.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Timing and material decisions are individualized and evidence is heterogeneous. The case is fictional and does not supply clinical advice. The multidisciplinary review describes uncertainty and preoperative planning.

practiceQuestions.stem: Fictional adult B has a sunken scalp flap and new concerns during rehabilitation after craniectomy. Which wording is most precise before postoperative response is known?

options.text: The syndrome of trephined is definitively confirmed.
A sunken-flap presentation warrants clinical assessment; the cited review reserves confirmation of syndrome of trephined for neurologic improvement after cranioplasty.
The finding proves infection.
The finding proves a specific implant is indicated.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The multidisciplinary review notes that the syndrome-of-trephined definition includes clinical resolution after cranioplasty; terminology should avoid premature certainty.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which pairing is correct for the Seddon classification?

options.text: Neurapraxia—myelin/conduction block; axonotmesis—axonal injury; neurotmesis—complete disruption.
Neurapraxia—complete transection; neurotmesis—transient block.
All terms mean the same injury.
The classifications describe cranioplasty materials.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The open peripheral nerve review summarizes Seddon and Sunderland classifications. This supplementary peripheral nerve content is not a declared Hopkins curriculum or an independent board track.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which consideration is most consistent with the Johns Hopkins neuroplastic approach pages?

options.text: Coordinate brain surgery with skull/scalp reconstruction planning to reduce or address contour problems, and consider the implant/device interface.
Only plan reconstruction after an aesthetic problem occurs.
A neuroplastic surgeon replaces the role of the neurosurgeon.
Every shunt must be embedded in a custom implant.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Hopkins describes joint preventive/reconstructive planning and multiple device-related clinical contexts; it does not require a single device strategy or replace neurosurgery.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 2019 Hopkins CME page awards credits for a live symposium. May a course author count those credits toward the 36-hour free-video floor?

options.text: Yes, because one CME credit always equals one public lecture-video hour.
Yes, even if the event was paid and no recording is available.
No; a historical live CME credit designation is not an observed, freely accessible recording runtime.
Yes, if the course name matches the fellowship.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Only free recordings with observed actual duration qualify. The event page describes a separately registered, historical live CME activity; the reviewed page did not provide a public lecture recording ledger.

title: Neurosurgery Residency Program
level: Clinical physician residency curriculum (independent, non-accredited educational self-study; not an actual residency)-aligned independent study
prerequisites: Advanced-level health-science knowledge equivalent to medical-school neuroscience, neuroanatomy, neurophysiology and clinical neurology; this is not beginner education.
Comfort with clinical terminology, evidence appraisal, neurologic examination concepts, CT/MR report interpretation and basic critical-care principles.

Learners must already hold appropriate professional training for any clinical activity. All cases and assignments here are self-study and do not authorize patient care, procedures or independent clinical decisions.
objectives: Integrate neuroanatomy, neurologic localization and time course into a qualified neurosurgical problem representation.
Compare neurosurgical syndromes across trauma, cerebrovascular, tumor, spine, pediatric, functional, skull-base/peripheral nerve and critical-care domains.
Describe broad interpretation limits of neuroimaging and pathology and identify when additional qualified review is needed.
Use evidence, guidelines and a differential diagnosis while separating observed data from inference and acknowledging uncertainty.
Communicate safe escalation, interdisciplinary collaboration and patient-safety reasoning in fictional vignettes.
Map self-study to public ABNS/CNS topic summaries without implying official blueprint completeness, exam readiness or probability of passing.

units.title: Neuroanatomy, localization, and the neurosurgical examination
objectives: Localize a lesion from a structured, time-linked neurologic history and examination without treating localization as diagnosis.
Relate vascular territories, cranial nerves, spinal tracts, ventricular anatomy and eloquent networks to common neurosurgical presentations.
State what missing information, urgent deterioration, or uncertainty should trigger escalation to a qualified clinical team.
topics: Cortical, deep, posterior fossa, brainstem and spinal cord localization; cranial nerves; long tracts; CSF spaces; focused exam; age and baseline context.
units.casePractice: Fictional oral-board vignette: map a focal deficit to two plausible neuroanatomic sites; list examination data that would discriminate them and one limitation.
units.assessment: One-page localization matrix graded for correct pathway, alternatives, time course, exam finding, uncertainty and safe escalation.

units.title: Neuroimaging, diagnostic reasoning, and evidence use
objectives: Describe a systematic approach to CT/MR sequences and vascular imaging without substituting for radiology interpretation.
Compare image findings with chronology, exam, prior studies and plausible mimics.
Communicate a differential and next information needed rather than anchoring on a single image.
topics: Noncontrast CT, MRI sequences, CTA/MRA/DSA concepts, postoperative imaging, artifact, incidental findings, neuroradiology collaboration, diagnostic uncertainty.
units.casePractice: Use a linked published case narrative (no downloaded image) to make a time-ordered evidence table and explain the tumor/vascular mimic differential.
units.assessment: Structured image-description exercise using only lawfully sourced teaching material or an instructor-cleared de-identified source; no diagnosis from invented synthetic imaging.

units.title: Neurotrauma, spinal injury, and evidence-based critical care
objectives: Distinguish primary injury, secondary injury and systemic threats as educational concepts.
Summarize the scope and limitations of severe-TBI guidance and recognize that local protocols and trained teams control care.
Present an organized escalation/consultation handoff for a hypothetical deteriorating patient.
topics: TBI mechanisms, intracranial hemorrhage, ICP concepts, spinal trauma, polytrauma, neurocritical care, evidence quality, serial reassessment.
units.casePractice: Fictional trauma sign-out: separate known facts from unknowns, identify immediate specialty-team escalation and outline the evidence source to check; no procedure/dose instruction.
units.assessment: Safety-critical handoff rubric: accurate timeline, red flags, uncertainty, escalation and no independent-treatment directions.

units.title: Cerebrovascular neurosurgery and neurovascular mimics
objectives: Organize the differential for hemorrhagic and ischemic presentations by syndrome, time course and vascular territory.
Explain aneurysm, AVM, dural AVF, cavernous malformation and moyamoya as distinct entities at a conceptual level.
Compare the role and limits of CT/CTA, MRI/MRA and catheter angiography in a team-based workup.
topics: SAH, ICH, aneurysms, AVM/AVF, dural fistula, ischemia, dissection, revascularization concepts, risk stratification and image review.
units.casePractice: Review the linked DAVF case report as a published example; outline the evolving differential and note what in the actual report must not be generalized.
units.assessment: Short oral-board style presentation scored for differential breadth, time course, evidence needs, multidisciplinary care and qualifiers.

units.title: Neuro-oncology, neuropathology, and decision frameworks
objectives: Connect symptoms, anatomy, imaging and pathology while acknowledging that classification and management change with evidence.
Distinguish broad lesion categories and identify where tissue/molecular data are needed.
Describe multidisciplinary decision factors without giving an individualized treatment plan.
topics: Primary and metastatic tumors, glioma, meningioma, sellar and skull-base lesions, pediatric tumors, pathology, molecular classification, biopsy/resection/radiosurgery concepts.
units.casePractice: Fictional tumor conference: make a problem representation from symptoms, imaging description and pathology status; list what is unresolved and who should collaborate.
units.assessment: Tumor board memo graded for anatomy, diagnosis qualifiers, missing evidence, shared decision factors and current-guideline checking.

units.title: Spinal neurosurgery across degenerative, traumatic, infectious, and neoplastic disease
objectives: Localize spinal cord, root and cauda equina syndromes and contrast urgent warning features with chronic patterns.
Describe imaging and stability questions that require trained clinical assessment.
Compare evidence and guideline scope for common spine presentations without proposing unsupervised surgery.
topics: Cervical/thoracolumbar degenerative disease, myelopathy, radiculopathy, cauda equina, fracture, infection, intradural/extradural tumor, deformity, peripheral nerve differential.
units.casePractice: Fictional progressive weakness and sphincter-symptom scenario: identify urgent escalation need and organize imaging/exam unknowns; do not give an operative plan.
units.assessment: Spine reasoning worksheet graded for localization, red flags, differential, imaging question, escalation and language scope.

units.title: Pediatric neurosurgery, CSF physiology, hydrocephalus, and congenital disease
objectives: Compare age-dependent presentation and developmental anatomy with adult assumptions.
Explain CSF circulation and distinguish communicating/obstructive patterns conceptually.
Use family-centered, multidisciplinary and safeguarding-aware reasoning in hypothetical pediatric scenarios.
topics: Hydrocephalus, shunt concerns, craniosynostosis, neural tube defects, pediatric tumors, congenital lesions, developmental neuroscience, pediatric trauma.
units.casePractice: Fictional child with new headache/vomiting and prior CSF diversion: construct a safe escalation and information checklist; no diagnostic certainty from one symptom.
units.assessment: Pediatric case presentation graded on age context, alternatives, urgency, caregiver communication and appropriate scope.

units.title: Functional neurosurgery, epilepsy, pain, and movement disorders
objectives: Explain high-level circuit concepts underlying epilepsy, movement disorders, pain and selected neuromodulation.
Describe candidate evaluation as multidisciplinary and dependent on diagnosis, goals, alternatives and risk review.
Differentiate education about devices/approaches from training to program or implant them.
topics: Epilepsy evaluation, functional networks, DBS concepts, neuromodulation, trigeminal neuralgia, spasticity, pain and ethical decision-making.
units.casePractice: Fictional multidisciplinary conference note for medication-refractory symptoms: articulate missing diagnostic, functional and patient-goal information before considering options.
units.assessment: Shared-decision concept map graded for indication uncertainty, alternatives, goals, risk discussion and no procedural competency claim.

units.title: Skull base, cranial nerves, peripheral nerve, and reconstructive interfaces
objectives: Relate skull-base compartments and cranial-nerve deficits to localization and differential diagnosis.
Distinguish peripheral nerve lesion patterns from root, plexus and central causes.
Identify cross-specialty collaboration and imaging/pathology details required for sound reasoning.
topics: Skull base anatomy, cranial neuropathies, vestibular schwannoma, pituitary/sellar and petroclival lesions, peripheral nerve injury/entrapment, reconstruction concepts.
units.casePractice: Fictional cranial-nerve localization exercise with two plausible skull-base sites and a plan for additional clinical data.
units.assessment: Anatomic map and differential graded for precision, alternate localization, evidence needs and team roles.

units.title: Perioperative systems, complications, infection, and neurocritical care
objectives: Recognize broad perioperative complication categories and why early team escalation, monitoring and communication matter.
Explain the distinction between a clinical guideline, institutional protocol and individual patient plan.
Use a systems-based morbidity review framework without directing clinical care.
topics: Pre-/post-operative assessment, neurologic change, infection, seizures, CSF leak, thromboembolism, ICU physiology, quality improvement and safe handoffs.
units.casePractice: Fictional postoperative safety huddle: separate event chronology, potential causes, immediate escalation, and systems factors; no patient-level orders.
units.assessment: Morbidity-review write-up scored for nonpunitive systems analysis, safety, uncertainty and guideline/protocol distinction.

units.title: Neurosurgical science, ethics, research methods, and lifelong learning
objectives: Interpret study design, bias, absolute/relative effects, uncertainty and external validity for neurosurgical decisions.
Discuss consent, privacy, image rights, conflicts and the limits of case reports.
Build a dated evidence search and update practice claims against current professional guidance.
topics: Evidence-based practice, clinical trials, observational evidence, diagnostic test properties, quality improvement, informed consent, equity, data privacy, publication rights.
units.casePractice: Critique a public case report and a guideline recommendation; label evidence level, dates, missing counterfactuals and copyright/privacy limits.
units.assessment: Evidence appraisal sheet graded for method, uncertainty, currency, applicability, citation and lawful use.

units.title: Integrated oral-board reasoning and cross-domain synthesis
objectives: Present a concise problem representation, differential, next information needs and safety-first team escalation.
Integrate trauma, vascular, tumor, spine, pediatric, functional, imaging, pathology and critical care concepts in novel vignettes.
Map self-study coverage to public ABNS/CNS topic summaries while recognizing unavailable proprietary materials and nonweighted public information.
topics: Simulated ED, clinic, ICU and postoperative scenarios; clinical judgment; alternatives; natural history; limitations; oral communication.
boardDomains: Primary exam areas reported by CNS
units.casePractice: Three original fictional oral-board style vignettes scored for reasoning, uncertainty, safe escalation and communication; no operative performance or patient-specific recommendations.
units.assessment: Capstone oral case + written self-audit, rubric-based formative feedback only; not validated, official or predictive of certification.

assignment.title: Integrated Neurosurgical Reasoning Portfolio (fictional education scenarios only)
deliverables: A localization/problem-representation worksheet for one fictional cranial and one fictional spine vignette.
A chronology and differential table that distinguishes reported findings, interpretation, missing evidence and uncertainty.
A guideline/evidence appraisal of one publicly linked CNS or Brain Trauma Foundation topic, including date, scope, certainty and limitations.
A case conference memo showing team roles, escalation and patient-safety communication without a real-patient treatment plan.
A board-domain coverage self-audit referencing ABNS/CNS public material; explicitly not a readiness or pass-probability prediction.
A rights/privacy checklist for any authentic case link. Do not copy medical images, patient records or protected content.
assignment.passingSuggestion: Formative suggestion only: 80% portfolio rubric with correction of every safety-critical reasoning error. This threshold is not validated, official, predictive, or a substitute for supervised assessment.

components: 12 unit-level retrieval exercises and fictional case analyses
Integrated portfolio with explicit grading rubric
Self-audit against public ABNS/CNS topic summaries
assessment.limitations: Original self-study items, not official or protected board content; not validated for board readiness or pass prediction; no clinical credential or scope is conveyed.

unitMap.text: Neuroanatomy, localization, and the neurosurgical examination
coveredTopics: Cortical, deep, posterior fossa, brainstem and spinal cord localization; cranial nerves; long tracts; CSF spaces; focused exam; age and baseline context.

unitMap.text: Neuroimaging, diagnostic reasoning, and evidence use
coveredTopics: Noncontrast CT, MRI sequences, CTA/MRA/DSA concepts, postoperative imaging, artifact, incidental findings, neuroradiology collaboration, diagnostic uncertainty.

unitMap.text: Neurotrauma, spinal injury, and evidence-based critical care
coveredTopics: TBI mechanisms, intracranial hemorrhage, ICP concepts, spinal trauma, polytrauma, neurocritical care, evidence quality, serial reassessment.

unitMap.text: Cerebrovascular neurosurgery and neurovascular mimics
coveredTopics: SAH, ICH, aneurysms, AVM/AVF, dural fistula, ischemia, dissection, revascularization concepts, risk stratification and image review.

unitMap.text: Neuro-oncology, neuropathology, and decision frameworks
coveredTopics: Primary and metastatic tumors, glioma, meningioma, sellar and skull-base lesions, pediatric tumors, pathology, molecular classification, biopsy/resection/radiosurgery concepts.

unitMap.text: Spinal neurosurgery across degenerative, traumatic, infectious, and neoplastic disease
coveredTopics: Cervical/thoracolumbar degenerative disease, myelopathy, radiculopathy, cauda equina, fracture, infection, intradural/extradural tumor, deformity, peripheral nerve differential.

unitMap.text: Pediatric neurosurgery, CSF physiology, hydrocephalus, and congenital disease
coveredTopics: Hydrocephalus, shunt concerns, craniosynostosis, neural tube defects, pediatric tumors, congenital lesions, developmental neuroscience, pediatric trauma.

unitMap.text: Functional neurosurgery, epilepsy, pain, and movement disorders
coveredTopics: Epilepsy evaluation, functional networks, DBS concepts, neuromodulation, trigeminal neuralgia, spasticity, pain and ethical decision-making.

unitMap.text: Skull base, cranial nerves, peripheral nerve, and reconstructive interfaces
coveredTopics: Skull base anatomy, cranial neuropathies, vestibular schwannoma, pituitary/sellar and petroclival lesions, peripheral nerve injury/entrapment, reconstruction concepts.

unitMap.text: Perioperative systems, complications, infection, and neurocritical care
coveredTopics: Pre-/post-operative assessment, neurologic change, infection, seizures, CSF leak, thromboembolism, ICU physiology, quality improvement and safe handoffs.

unitMap.text: Neurosurgical science, ethics, research methods, and lifelong learning
coveredTopics: Evidence-based practice, clinical trials, observational evidence, diagnostic test properties, quality improvement, informed consent, equity, data privacy, publication rights.

unitMap.text: Integrated oral-board reasoning and cross-domain synthesis
coveredTopics: Simulated ED, clinic, ICU and postoperative scenarios; clinical judgment; alternatives; natural history; limitations; oral communication.

All existing original clip targets remain planned only; no target minutes or authored scripts are rendered or included in verified recording hours.

medical.trackType: Clinical physician residency curriculum (independent, non-accredited educational self-study; not an actual residency)
boardNames: American Board of Neurological Surgery (ABNS): Primary Examination and Oral Examination route to ABNS diplomate certification
American Osteopathic Board of Surgery (AOBS): Neurological Surgery Written Qualifying Exam (or ABNS qualifying exam accepted by AOBS) followed by AOBS Oral Exam and AOA approval
medical.boardStatus: A distinct physician specialty board-certification pathway exists. ABNS identifies its primary examination as a required step and its oral examination as the final certification step after board-defined accredited training, primary-exam, practice/log, application and other requirements. ABNS says the primary examination is 375 MCQs and requires mastery of its neuroanatomy exam before primary-exam credit since July 1, 2025. A separate osteopathic certification route also exists: AOBS administers its own written and oral examinations, and accepts the ABNS qualifying exam as one route to its oral exam; AOA approval is separate. These credentials are not interchangeable and are not combined in this course. No public weighted ABNS content blueprint was recovered; broad domains are mapped using the CNS public summary and ABNS oral topics. ABNS primary page had a stale March 7, 2025 schedule line at the 2026-10-07 check, so no current exam date is stated.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: This course grants no ABNS or AOBS exam eligibility, credential, certification or credit. ABNS eligibility is controlled by the board and includes completion of an 84-month ACGME-approved residency, examination and subsequent practice/case-log/application requirements; the oral examination is a later step. AOBS eligibility and AOA approval are separately determined under current AOBS/AOA rules. Verify current requirements directly with the board. No passing outcome is guaranteed.

topicGaps: Observed lecture runtime now exceeds the old zero-hour ledger: 42.319 unique external hours across 46 new public University of Utah Grand Rounds recordings. The 36-hour floor is met; residual is 0.000 hours. This does not establish clinical competency, board readiness, or complete blueprint coverage.
All existing original clip targets remain planned only; no target minutes or authored scripts are rendered or included in verified recording hours.
The public ABNS Primary Examination page links its keyword guide through MyABNS; no public weighted blueprint was recovered. CNS subject areas are broad, not weighted or exhaustive.
The Johns Hopkins public PGY-5/6/7 schedule summary overlaps research and chief-year wording; local rotation calendar remains unconfirmed.

Coverage still needs qualified faculty teaching or further vetted resources for full cranial/skull-base and peripheral-nerve examination, pediatric CSF, neurocritical care, perioperative systems, practical image interpretation, and integrated oral reasoning. Recorded grand rounds are selected talks, not a complete course or residency.

Grand Rounds content is archived in 2020–2025, so claims about treatment standards may be historical; pair with current CNS/other relevant guidelines and verify dates before teaching practice. The course includes links, not copied media, and does not infer re-use or embedding rights.
The NREF/AANS Endovascular-Vascular catalog record remains a free course listing, not a verified individual recording ledger; it contributes zero hours.
medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional adult develops abrupt diplopia, dysarthria, and limb ataxia. Which reasoning step is most appropriate before assigning a single lesion diagnosis?

options.text: Localize the pattern, establish exact onset and associated findings, and seek urgent evaluation by the qualified clinical team.
Assume a single named artery is occluded from these three symptoms alone.
Conclude the symptoms are functional because multiple systems are involved.
Treat a normal screening exam as excluding posterior fossa disease.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The cluster suggests a potentially central process, but syndrome localization is not etiologic confirmation. Time course and focused exam/imaging reviewed by the care team matter; do not overclaim from a short vignette.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient with head trauma becomes less responsive during observation. In a self-study case exercise, what is the safest educationally appropriate next action?

options.text: Continue the planned routine assessment because the first examination was reassuring.
Promptly escalate the change to the responsible emergency/neurosurgical team and follow local emergency protocol.
Infer a specific hematoma type without further evaluation.
Use a public lecture as a substitute for bedside reassessment.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Neurologic deterioration is a safety signal requiring immediate qualified clinical evaluation and local protocol; the course does not supply patient-level orders or diagnoses.

practiceQuestions.stem: A published case report describes temporal symptoms and evolving edema initially concerning for a tumor, with later imaging revealing abnormal vascular structures. What general cognitive lesson is best supported?

options.text: Atypical imaging can require a revisited differential and multidisciplinary review; a single initial label should not end reasoning.
All temporal lesions with seizures are dural fistulas.
A case report establishes a universal imaging algorithm.
A single metabolic imaging value proves tumor biology.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The linked report illustrates one mimic and evolving evidence; a case report is not a prevalence estimate or universal rule. This course links, but does not reproduce, the case images.

practiceQuestions.stem: In a fictional case, a person with back symptoms reports new saddle sensory change and bladder dysfunction. Which response best demonstrates safe reasoning for an educational learner?

options.text: Treat as a routine chronic pain follow-up because imaging can wait.
Recognize potential time-sensitive neurologic compromise and urgently involve qualified clinical services under local protocol.
Name the exact lesion and prescribe a procedure from symptoms alone.
Reassure that preserved ankle movement rules out serious pathology.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The symptoms warrant urgent clinician assessment; the vignette does not establish a diagnosis or authorize treatment. Clinical protocols govern real care.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional child with prior CSF diversion develops a new change in alertness and recurrent vomiting. What is the best course-level interpretation?

options.text: A prior device means symptoms are expected and can be ignored.
The presentation needs prompt assessment by the responsible pediatric/neurosurgical team; multiple causes remain possible.
The shunt is definitely obstructed and a specific intervention is indicated.
A normal temperature excludes a device or neurologic problem.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The symptoms in a child with a CSF device merit urgent qualified assessment, but they do not establish shunt malfunction or any intervention. Do not use this self-study vignette to triage a real child.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner receives an imaging description of a suspected brain mass, but no tissue or molecular findings. Which statement is most defensible?

options.text: A definitive integrated tumor classification can always be assigned from a brief imaging description.
Maintain a differential and state that classification/management may depend on pathology, molecular data, clinical context, and current guidance.
Assume the lesion is metastatic because primary tumors are rare.
Use the most common histology as the diagnosis for every patient.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Imaging alone may not establish an integrated diagnosis. The appropriate level of certainty depends on clinical, radiologic, pathologic and molecular evidence and current standards.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement accurately distinguishes ABNS certification stages from this independent curriculum?

options.text: Completing this curriculum grants ABNS board eligibility.
ABNS lists a primary examination and a later oral examination with board-controlled training/practice requirements; this curriculum grants neither eligibility nor certification.
The ABNS primary exam alone automatically awards diplomate status.
A CNS course certificate substitutes for ACGME residency.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABNS describes a multistep pathway with required accredited training, primary exam, subsequent practice/log/application requirements and oral exam. An independent educational course is not accredited training or a credential.

practiceQuestions.stem: A single published neurosurgical case report describes a favorable outcome after a treatment. What can reasonably be inferred?

options.text: The treatment is proven superior for all comparable patients.
The report can generate a learning question and illustrate a possible presentation, but cannot establish comparative efficacy or generalizable frequency.
The absence of a control group makes the report useful only if the image is copied.
The reported outcome eliminates publication bias.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Case reports are useful for hypothesis generation and pattern recognition but lack a comparator and do not support broad causal efficacy estimates.

practiceQuestions.stem: A public case article displays MRI figures and says the journal uses a Creative Commons Attribution license. What should an instructor do before putting a figure into a course slide?

options.text: Assume free-to-view means public domain.
Verify the individual article/figure license and required attribution, check for patient identifiers/consent concerns, and use only if permitted; otherwise link rather than copy.
Remove the caption and reuse the image without attribution.
Crop the patient's face and the image is automatically de-identified and reusable.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A general journal license does not remove the need for item-level rights and privacy review. This course uses links only and does not copy patient images.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which set most closely reflects the public CNS summary of ABNS Primary Examination coverage?

options.text: Only operative technique videos and memorized instruments.
Basic sciences, critical care, clinical skills, imaging, neuroanatomy, neurobiology, neurology, neuropharmacology, neurosurgery, pathology and related disciplines.
Only subspecialty fellowship topics selected by each hospital.
Only the topics listed on one residency website.

practiceQuestions.rationale: CNS lists these broad domains. The ABNS primary resource's current keyword guide is not a public weighted blueprint in the reviewed pages, so no percent weights are invented.

practiceQuestions.stem: A trainee is asked to distinguish conductive from sensorineural loss using audiology. Which pairing most directly supports a conductive component?

options.text: Air-bone gap on audiometry
Elevated bone thresholds with no air-bone gap
Absent vestibular-evoked myogenic potential alone
Abnormal facial nerve EMG alone

practiceQuestions.rationale: An air-bone gap is a pattern supporting conductive hearing loss; interpretation requires the complete audiologic context and cannot be inferred from a single unrelated vestibular or facial test.

ANS fellowship directory

Order imaging for every presentation without clinical context

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2020 AAO-HNS guideline concerns adults with suspected definite/probable disease and aims to improve diagnostic accuracy while reducing unindicated testing. Symptoms alone or a single test should not be treated as conclusive.

Monitoring is an adjunct whose signals require context and qualified interpretation

topicGaps: As of 2026-10-07, 3.765111 observed and accessible recording hours are counted: 2.650667 specialty hours and 1.114444 shared foundation hours. The 36-hour video target retains a 32.234889-hour unfilled gap. Target minutes and unrendered clip plans are not rendered media or verified hours.

Verified recordings cluster in sleep-disordered breathing, test-selection/actigraphy and broad sleep-health foundation. No full-length individually runtime-verified recording was found in this pass for much of the blueprint, including insomnia, central hypersomnolence, parasomnias, sleep-related movement disorders and pediatric breadth.

The official AASM archive lists additional relevant webinars, but sampled individual Vimeo pages returned a human-verification challenge without playable runtime metadata. These remain uncounted and unverified; no challenge was bypassed.

The AASM breathing-disorders video is an educational overview, not current treatment authority. Use the current AASM guideline index and linked guidelines for adult/pediatric recommendations and updates.
Five original source-grounded teaching episodes are authored as scripts only. They are not rendered, hosted or counted; further production is required to close the media gap.

Public curricula and blueprint mappings do not establish clinical competency or board eligibility. Accredited clinical fellowship, supervised practice and human clinician review remain separate and are not replaced.

No separate institutional track was established from public sources. Preserve the clinical programme variant exactly as listed above.
sourceCaveats: The ACGME document is a program-accreditation requirement, not the Hopkins private didactic schedule.
The ABIM blueprint is one joint exam specification; board-specific eligibility differs. Board co-sponsors are named as in ABIM’s current policy (ABO is rendered as ABOHNS there).
The 2025 AASM combination-insomnia guideline is current at time checked; source says the evidence search ended June 2025. Recheck current guidance before clinical application.
ACGME and board policy can change. Follow each official source rather than relying on this self-study curriculum.
AASM case-study pages were public only as a catalogue; sampled full case article was member-exclusive and is not required. Human Sleep Project requires credentialing and a signed DUA.

Stateless YouTube metadata was blocked by sign-in/bot verification and was not bypassed. Panopto archive descriptions were approximately one hour but lack observed individual durations. Harvard APNEA index lists brief durations; canonical media identifiers and playback were not verified.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional adult has loud snoring, witnessed pauses, sleepiness, and hypertension, without major cardiopulmonary disease, opioid use, stroke, severe insomnia, or suspected hypoventilation. Which diagnostic path is guideline-concordant?

options.text: A questionnaire alone establishes OSA
PSG or technically adequate HSAT may be used after comprehensive evaluation
Start PAP without testing
Use MSLT as the first test

practiceQuestions.rationale: In an uncomplicated adult with increased risk for moderate-to-severe OSA, PSG or technically adequate HSAT is appropriate. Questionnaires do not diagnose OSA.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient with chronic opioid exposure and suspected sleep-related hypoventilation has snoring and sleepiness. Which test is preferred for OSA evaluation?

options.text: HSAT as the default
Attended PSG rather than HSAT
Sleep diary only
Overnight oximetry alone

practiceQuestions.rationale: The guideline prefers PSG over HSAT when chronic opioid use or suspected hypoventilation raises risk for non-obstructive breathing disorders.

practiceQuestions.stem: A technically adequate HSAT in a fictional symptomatic patient is negative, but clinical suspicion remains. What is the next diagnostic step?

options.text: Declare OSA excluded
Repeat questionnaire only
Perform PSG
Begin empiric stimulant therapy

practiceQuestions.rationale: A single negative, inconclusive, or technically inadequate HSAT should be followed by PSG when concern persists.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional adult reports persistent insomnia and requests a medication-only plan. What best reflects current AASM recommendations?

options.text: CBT-I has no role
CBT-I is an evidence-based behavioral treatment; 2025 guideline conditionally favors CBT-I plus medication over medication alone, but not over CBT-I alone
Combination treatment is mandatory for all
Sleep hygiene alone is equivalent to CBT-I

practiceQuestions.rationale: AASM recommends behavioral/psychological treatments and the 2025 combination guideline makes conditional comparisons; decisions are individualized.

practiceQuestions.stem: Before a planned MSLT for a fictional patient with sleepiness, what is an important prerequisite?

options.text: No PSG is required
Document adequate/stable sleep schedule and obtain preceding attended PSG with sufficient sleep opportunity
Stop all medications without clinician oversight
Perform MSLT immediately after PAP titration

practiceQuestions.rationale: Protocol guidance emphasizes sleep schedule documentation, preparation, and a preceding attended PSG; medication changes require clinical oversight.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional adult reports an urge to move the legs, worse at rest in the evening, relieved by movement. Which next step is supported by current RLS guidance?

options.text: Assume PLMD from symptoms alone
Check regular iron studies and review exacerbating factors
Order HSAT for diagnosis
Start chronic dopamine agonist automatically

practiceQuestions.rationale: AASM good-practice statement calls for iron studies and addressing alcohol, caffeine, relevant medications and untreated OSA; treatment is individualized and augmentation matters.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient has dream-enactment behavior with potentially injurious movements. Which diagnostic feature supports RBD?

options.text: Loss of REM atonia on PSG
High AHI on HSAT
Short MSLT latency alone
Elevated ferritin

practiceQuestions.rationale: RBD diagnosis requires clinical features and PSG demonstration of REM sleep without atonia; evaluate mimics and safety.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional child is evaluated for suspected OSA. Which learning principle is most appropriate?

options.text: Adult HSAT rules automatically transfer to children
Use pediatric-specific evaluation and PSG guidance; do not assume adult pathways apply
A normal questionnaire excludes OSA
A diagnosis can be made from snoring alone

practiceQuestions.rationale: Pediatric sleep evaluation and test protocols have age-specific standards; symptoms alone do not establish a diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional adult complains of unrefreshing sleep, but sleep timing shifts later by about an hour across repeated weeks. Which information is most useful before assigning a circadian diagnosis?

options.text: Single-night PSG alone
Longitudinal sleep diary with actigraphy when appropriate
One screening questionnaire
A single serum melatonin measurement without timing

practiceQuestions.rationale: Longitudinal timing patterns help evaluate circadian rhythm disorders; sleep diaries/actigraphy are useful adjuncts and must be interpreted in context.
